newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE-Bored rubber traders wait for Malaysia market to turn.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bored rubber traders wait for Malaysia market to turn.

text.p: It's 10 a.m. and David has just whiled away 30 minutes in his office, chatting to someone in Bangkok about the weather and sports cars. Now he's absorbed in a computer game where he saves a beautiful girl shipwrecked on an island populated by savages.
At noon he goes to lunch, and on his return, ponders how to pass the afternoon.
Nice work if you can get it.
Dozens of Malaysian rubber traders like David are finding ways to keep busy in the office as the rubber market in the world's third largest grower of the crop languishes.

"I can count the number of days that I've actually done any trading this year," said David, who did not want his full name to be used or his company to be identified. "How can you sell when there's no one to buy?"
PRICE SQUEEZE
Malaysian rubber industry officials blame European, Far East and U.S. importers, who consume most of the rubber produced by the country, for depressing prices.
These importers, who act for manufacturers of tyres, gloves, condoms and other rubber products, persistently tried to buy below production cost, the officials said.
The price of Standard Malaysian Rubber (SMR) has fallen by about six percent in the past six months to an average of 315 Malaysian/Singapore cents a kg.
Competition from Indonesia, which usually quotes 10 to 20 Malaysian cents lower for its rubber, is also eating into sales.
THREATEN CONSUMERS

The officials said it would be difficult for Malaysian rubber factories and growers to stay in business if the price -- a weighted average of the Singapore and Malaysian currencies -- dipped below 300 cents.

"If there is no fair and remunerative price for rubber, then producers will be forced to cut back on production and rubber prices will spiral like nobody's business," Malaysian Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik said recently.

Lim said he did not wish to threaten consumers. "But they should know that our economies are undergoing structural changes and we're growing less dependent on rubber and turning to other lucrative crops," he said.
SUPPLY AND DEMAND
Buyers say supply and demand factors dictate the price.

"We are not doing anything to squeeze prices," said a Singapore-based purchasing manager for a U.S. tyre company. "If I can get SIR (Standard Indonesian Rubber) at a cheaper price, why should I buy the SMR for more?

Another purchasing official for a European tyre maker in Singapore said rubber markets were feeling the pinch from a global slowdown in auto manufacturing and assembling, which has suppressed the need for tyres and rubber parts.
"Seventy percent of the world's rubber now goes into the auto industry and as a consequence, the commodity is suffering," said the official.
INRO BUFFER STOCK

The International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO), which intervenes in the market to support rubber prices, raised its reference or neutral price for interventions by four percent to 206.68 Malaysian/Singapore cents last month.
James Hegarty, INRO's buffer stock manager, said the increase reflected higher rubber prices since last year.
"Certainly, one will see consumption start to increase later this year but I'm not going to make a forecast," he said.
WAITING GAME
In the meantime, traders fend off boredom waiting for the market to turn.

"Usually, I try and get in a customer every day," said a rubber trader with a foreign-owned commodities house in Kuala Lumpur. "After reading the Reuters screen and whatever statistics, I'm ready to make my offer."
"Then starts the waiting game -- whether they're ready to buy."
When there is a deal it's usually not very big.
"If there's anything traded out of the Malaysian market today, it's usually small parcels of around 100 tonnes each," said one trader.
Another said: "I've played all the games in Windows. Last week, I started chasing bad debts for the company."
DO BETTER IN RICE
One trader said he had been talking with a colleague in Thailand about going into rice trading.
"We talked a lot about the (rubber) market and found it was heading nowhere," said the trader. "My friend is convinced we'll do better in rice."
For the bigger commodity houses dealing in rubber, the past six months have been an ideal time to send staff on seminars, product training and visits to offices of overseas clients.
"It's when we become ambassadors of goodwill for the company," said a rubber trader with a multinational commodities firm in Kuala Lumpur, after a week's trip to China.
"When you're a big company dealing in various commodity products, it's also easier," said the trader. "You can always count on other crops."

Traders said despite the market lethargy, small trading companies could still stay in rubber, although not indefinitely. "Sooner or later, the market must rebound. Otherwise, you could see some diversification," said a trader.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230-7509)
